DARK
IMPERIUM
PLAYER'S HANDBOOK

DARK IMPERIUM
A thousand wars await
“In the grim darkness of the far future, there is only war.”
— Warhammer 40,000
Above the hive, the stars disappear behind the smoke of another burning district. Below, a million 
workers report for their shifts. The guns on the walls have not stopped firing in six days. The morning 
broadcast calls this a victory.
Across the Imperium, lives are spent to hold worlds whose names their defenders can barely 
pronounce. A transport arrives carrying fresh soldiers and leaves with sealed casualty ledgers. In the 
chapel beside the embarkation gate, someone has scratched a name into the stone beneath every 
candle.
Now the Great Rift scars the heavens. Beyond it, messages fail and relief fleets become rumours. A 
governor may rule for years without learning whether the authority that appointed them still exists. A 
distress call may arrive long after everyone who sent it is dead.
Your warband works where the grand proclamations end: in a flooded transit tunnel, aboard a silent 
freighter, outside a door that should never have been opened. You have your weapons, your orders 
and the people beside you. None of them is entirely reliable.
You may never save a world. You can still bring someone home. Decide whose name you will 
remember, what you will refuse to become, and what you are willing to risk when the next order comes.
ABOUT THE GALAXY SPREAD
An illustrative, unofficial post-Rift atlas. World positions and storm shapes are approximate; the chart shows selected landmarks, not 
territorial control or navigable routes. The five segmenta are administrative regions, not five separate empires.
Lore references: Warhammer 40,000 — The Setting (warhammer40000.com/the-setting); Warhammer Community — The lore of 
Armageddon (3 June 2026); Lexicanum — Galaxy (8th Edition), for comparative geography. Checked October 2026.

1
SECTION 01
Dark Imperium
The dock bells have been sounding for an hour. Beyond the glass, a warship waits among the gantries, its 
armoured flanks disappearing into shadow. Below it, a clerk counts the people crossing the embarkation 
bridge. He has been given a quota, not their names.
Somewhere inside that ship is an order bearing your destination. There may be a village to defend, a 
missing patrol to find, or a sealed door that must never open. The galaxy will scarcely notice whether you 
return. The people beside you will.

2
1 Dark Imperium
Dark Imperium is a grimdark d20 warband roleplaying game built on a familiar 5e-style rules chassis and adapted for 
firefights, armour, suppression, dangerous psychic power, factional authority and the brutal scale of the 41st 
Millennium.
This Player's Handbook contains the rules a player needs to create, advance and run a character. Enemy construction, 
encounter budgets, campaign fronts, patron procedures and other behind-the-screen systems belong in the Game 
Master's Guide or Bestiary.
This is an unofficial fan-made conversion for private tabletop play. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by Games 
Workshop, Wizards of the Coast, or their licensors.
1.1 Design Goals
● Brutal but heroic.
● Tactical without becoming simulation-heavy.
● Grimdark without making player choices meaningless.
● Built around ranged combat, cover, faith, corruption and dangerous psychic power.
● Playable with mixed warbands of soldiers, zealots, psykers, abhumans, enforcers, scum and Mechanicus operatives.
● Fast enough to run at a normal tabletop while still making equipment and battlefield position matter.
1.2 Core System
Dark Imperium uses a familiar d20 rules chassis for ability checks, attack rolls, saving throws, Armour Class, initiative, 
actions and reactions. The Player's Handbook defines the player-facing procedures most often needed during play, 
including range, cover, suppression, opportunity attacks, grappling, rests and conditions. When an edge case is not 
covered here, the GM makes a ruling using the closest existing procedure, with additional campaign and encounter 
guidance in the Game Master's Guide.
1.3 Character Tiers
Tier Levels Typical Scope
Tier 1 1-4 Districts, facilities, local threats and small warband operations.
Tier 2 5-10 Planetary operations, elite enemies and major institutional conflict.
Tier 3 11-16 System or subsector crises, powerful relics and strategic enemies.
Tier 4 17-20 Sector-changing operations, armies, catastrophic Warp threats and legendary 
characters.
1.4 Proficiency Bonus
Levels Proficiency Bonus
1-4 +2
5-8 +3
9-12 +4
13-16 +5
17-20 +6
1.5 Rules Priority
1. Use the most recent Player's Handbook for player-
facing character rules.
2. Use a dedicated Bestiary stat block over an older 
conversion or improvised profile.
3. A specific feature overrides a general rule when the 
two conflict.
4. When two equally specific rules conflict, use the newer 
version and record the issue for the next revision.
5. When no rule applies, the GM makes a ruling using 
the closest existing procedure and play continues.

SECTION 02
Character Creation
The clerk asks for your name twice. The first time, he cannot hear it over the engines. The second, he is 
checking it against a list of the missing. You watch his finger stop on a line and wonder which answer would 
have been safer.
Behind you, the next recruit shifts beneath a borrowed coat. Ahead, a door opens onto the mustering deck. 
Whatever brought you here has left its marks: a regimental habit, an old debt, a prayer learned at home. 
Soon, strangers will depend on what you have carried with you.

2 Character Creation
Create a character in the following order. Most 
campaigns begin at level 3, but the rules support levels 
1-20.
1. Choose Species.
2. Choose Origin.
3. Generate ability scores.
4. Choose Class.
5. Choose one Universal Trait.
6. Record proficiencies, saving throws and class 
features.
7. Choose starting equipment.
8. Calculate Armour Class, hit points, attack modifiers 
and save DCs.
9. Name the character, define their warband role and 
establish why they are working with the group.
2.1 Ability Scores
Use the ability-score method chosen for the campaign. 
The default method is the standard array: 15, 14, 13, 12, 
10, 8, assigned before species bonuses. Point buy or 
rolled scores may be used with GM approval.
2.2 Hit Points
At level 1, gain the maximum value of your class Hit Die 
+ your Constitution modifier. At later levels, either roll the 
Hit Die or use the fixed value: d6 = 4, d8 = 5, d10 = 6, 
d12 = 7, then add your Constitution modifier. Species 
and class features may alter your maximum hit points.
2.3 Species and Class Restrictions
Species Available Classes Notes
Human Veteran, Zealot, Psyker, Arbites 
Enforcer, Hive Scum Most flexible Imperial species.
Ogryn Ogryn Skullbreaker Class-locked; variety comes from Ogryn 
roles and talents.
Ratling Ratling Sharpshooter, Veteran, Hive 
Scum
Sniper, scout, thief, cook and rogue-style 
specialist.
Skitarii Skitarii Veteran Mechanicus-only; no psychic access.
Squat / Kin Kin Armsman, Hernkyn Prospector Tough, technically capable specialist; 
rare in Imperial warbands.
Aeldari / Eldar Aeldari Outcast, Aeldari Warlock Xenos option for unusual campaigns; 
should require a strong narrative reason.

Charisma Medium

Optional campaign restriction: in a strictly Imperial 
campaign, Squats/Kin may appear as sanctioned allies 
while Aeldari are normally NPCs or exceptional guest 
characters.
2.4 Hard Restrictions
2.4.1 Ogryns
Ogryns may only take the Ogryn Skullbreaker class.
They cannot be Veterans, Zealots, Psykers, Arbites, Hive 
Scum, Skitarii, or Ratling Sharpshooters. Ogryn
variety comes from Ogryn subclasses, not from normal 
class choice.
2.4.2 Skitarii
Skitarii cannot be Psykers. They may only take the 
Skitarii Veteran class.
Skitarii are cybernetically altered, doctrinally conditioned, 
and tied to the Machine Cult. Their identity
should stay separate from psychic characters, faith-
driven zealots, underhive scum, and normal
Imperial soldiers.
2.4.3 Psykers
Psykers are Human-only in the core player rules.
No Ogryn Psykers, Ratling Psykers, or Skitarii Psykers 
are available to player characters. Rare
exceptions may exist as NPCs, mutants, villains, or 
campaign-specific threats.
2.4.4 Ratlings
Ratlings are not just small humans. They are best suited 
to sniping, scouting, stealth, infiltration,
smuggling, spotting targets, and surviving through luck 
and cowardice.
Ratlings may be Ratling Sharpshooters, Veterans, or 
Hive Scum. They cannot normally be Psykers,
Arbites, Skitarii, Ogryns, or standard Zealots.

A rare Ratling Zealot can exist with GM approval, but 
should use modified ranged faith features rather
than heavy melee features.
2.4.5 Squats / Kin
Squats, also called Kin in many modern Imperial records, 
are not simply short humans. They are dense,
hardy, void-adapted, stubborn, and culturally bound to 
clan, hold, oath, guild, and ancestor-core
traditions.
Squats/Kin may be Kin Armsmen or Hernkyn 
Prospectors. They cannot be Psykers, Zealots, Arbites,
Skitarii, Ogryns, Ratling Sharpshooters, or Aeldari 
classes.
A Squat/Kin character in an Imperial warband should 
have a clear reason for cooperation: a trade
contract, mercenary oath, salvage claim, ancient grudge, 
debt, diplomatic mission, or shared enemy.
2.4.6 Aeldari / Eldar
Aeldari are xenos and should not be treated as normal 
Imperial citizens. They are included for
campaigns where the GM wants uneasy alliances, 
temporary warband cooperation, corsair contact,
ranger intervention, or a story built around a greater 
threat.
Aeldari may be Aeldari Outcasts or Aeldari Warlocks. 
They cannot take Imperial classes, Ogryn classes,
Ratling classes, Squat/Kin classes, or Skitarii classes.
An Aeldari Warlock should normally be a former Seer 
who has walked the Path of the Warrior. A lone
Warlock travelling with an Imperial warband needs a 
strong narrative hook, such as a Farseer
command, a hidden webway objective, a daemon threat, 
or a necessary but temporary alliance.
2.5 Skills and Ability Checks
When a task has an uncertain outcome, roll d20 + the 
relevant ability modifier. If you are proficient in the skill or 
tool that applies, also add your proficiency bonus. A 
saving throw uses the same structure, adding proficiency 
only when your class or another rule grants proficiency in 
that saving throw.
Advantage and disadvantage: roll two d20s and use the 
higher result for advantage or the lower result for 
disadvantage. Multiple sources of the same type do not 
stack; if you have both advantage and disadvantage, 
they cancel, and you roll one d20.
Skill Ability Typical Use
Acrobatics Dexterity Balance, controlled movement and 
physical agility.
Athletics Strength
Climbing, jumping, grappling, 
shoving, swimming and forcing 
obstacles.
Investigation Intelligen
ce
Searching scenes, analysing 
evidence and piecing clues 
together.
Medicine Wisdom Stabilisation, diagnosis, field 
treatment and medicae equipment.
Perception Wisdom Spotting threats, movement, hidden 
objects and ambushes.
Stealth Dexterity Moving quietly, hiding, infiltration 
and avoiding observation.
Skill Ability Typical Use
Survival Wisdom Tracking, navigation, shelter, 
supplies and hostile environments.
Technology Intelligen
ce
Cogitators, auspexes, locks, 
machinery and technical analysis.
Other skills use the same procedure. Deception, 
Intimidation and Persuasion normally use Charisma; 
Insight uses Wisdom; History and Religion use 
Intelligence; Sleight of Hand uses Dexterity. The GM may 
pair a skill with a different ability when the approach 
changes, such as Strength (Intimidation) for a physical 
display of force.

SECTION 03
Species
The meeting takes place beyond the station patrols. An Ogryn stoops beneath the lintel while a Ratling 
searches the corners. The hooded Skitarii turns towards a sound nobody else can hear. Across the chest, a 
Kin envoy waits for the human to finish speaking. The Aeldari has offered neither a name nor a promise.
Their patron has arranged one journey together. That is all. Each brings a different measure of danger, 
loyalty and obligation; each has reasons to leave. For now, the same enemy waits beyond the next airlock.

SPECIES LORE
Human and Ogryn
3.1 Human
Humanity lives beneath the weight of an empire too 
vast for any one person to comprehend. A hive 
labourer, a shipborn deckhand and a shrine pilgrim 
may share devotion to the Emperor while knowing 
almost nothing of one another's lives. Their 
customs, accents and fears are shaped by the 
place that raised them.
Imperial institutions demand obedience and service, 
but a person's loyalties can be much smaller and 
more stubborn: the family left in a hab-block, the 
friend who shared a ration, the squad whose names 
are scratched inside a helmet. Such attachments 
can sustain someone whom the authorities regard 
as replaceable.
In a warband, a human might be a career soldier, a 
survivor of the streets, a believer or a reluctant 
specialist. Decide what your character misses about 
home, and which lesson from that life they still trust. 
A familiar habit can reveal more than a long 
account of past victories.
3.2 Ogryn Abhuman
Ogryns are immense abhumans whose strength 
and endurance make them valuable to Imperial 
armies and heavy industry. Their equipment must 
withstand bodies and hands far larger than those of 
ordinary humans. On the battlefield they may carry 
brutal weapons, shield their comrades, or force a 
passage through a position others cannot breach.
The Imperium often judges an Ogryn by how much 
they can carry or destroy. A warband has time to 
learn the person behind that judgement: a carefully 
remembered promise, pride in a trusted duty, or the 
quiet certainty that a smaller companion must be 
kept safe. Loyalty can be deeply personal even 
when the order that first inspired it was simple.
Give your Ogryn something they take seriously 
beyond fighting. They may keep an exact count of 
their companions, preserve a gift from an old 
commander, or insist that nobody is left behind. 
Their way of understanding a problem can be direct 
without making their feelings shallow.

SPECIES LORE
Ratling and Skitarii
3.3 Ratling Abhuman
Ratlings are small, hardy abhumans whose sharp 
senses and marksmanship have earned them a 
place in Imperial armies. Their stature makes many 
human spaces awkward, but offers advantages 
wherever concealment matters. A ruined building 
that exposes an ordinary soldier may hold a dozen 
comfortable hiding places for a Ratling.
Life among taller comrades can involve affection, 
prejudice and the constant expectation of mischief. 
A particular Ratling might cultivate that reputation, 
resent it, or use it to divert attention from something 
more important. Food, favours and useful 
information can sustain relationships that rank 
alone cannot secure.
Consider who first trusted your character with a 
difficult job. They may take pride in feeding a 
squad, finding an overlooked route, or making a 
seemingly impossible shot. Give them a private 
ambition as well as a useful trick; being 
underestimated is an experience, not a complete 
personality.
3.4 Skitarii Augmented Human
Skitarii are the augmented soldiery of the Adeptus 
Mechanicus. Beneath robes and armour, flesh is 
joined to machinery in service to the Machine God. 
Their altered senses and disciplined routines reflect 
a life shaped by forge worlds, sacred maintenance 
and commands carried through systems others 
cannot perceive.
The extent of augmentation and personal 
independence varies. A warrior may remember an 
earlier name, regard a replacement limb as a 
blessing, or understand duty through streams of 
information that arrive without a spoken word. A 
damaged component can be both a practical 
burden and a source of religious unease.
Away from a larger force, a Skitarius must negotiate 
unfamiliar people and incomplete instructions. 
Decide which ritual still anchors your character 
when communications fail. In this handbook, Skitarii 
occupy a species entry for character creation, but 
they remain augmented humans rather than a 
separate biological species.

SPECIES LORE
Kin and Aeldari
3.5 Squat / Kin
The Kin build their lives around kindred, work and 
inherited obligation. The Leagues of Votann guard 
immense stores of ancestral knowledge within their 
revered Ancestor Cores. Survival in hostile 
environments encourages careful preparation, 
reliable craftsmanship and a long memory for debts 
owed or harms done.
The name Squat is also associated with 
communities such as Necromunda's Ironhead 
prospectors. Those mining clans have their own 
history and local traditions; a character need not be 
a recent arrival from a League. Decide whether 
home means a distant Hold, an industrial settlement 
or the cramped working decks of an expedition 
vessel.
A Kin traveller may carry a contract, a family tool or 
a promise whose importance outsiders struggle to 
understand. Their place in a warband can grow 
through dependable work and reciprocal trust. Ask 
what they hope to bring home: wealth, knowledge, 
an honoured name, or someone who should never 
have been lost.
3.6 Aeldari / Eldar
The Aeldari inherit the memory of an empire 
destroyed by its own excess. For those of the 
craftworlds, disciplined Paths offer a way to contain 
the intensity of thought and emotion that helped 
bring about the Fall. Spirit stones and the 
preservation of the dead are bound to survival as 
well as tradition.
An Outcast has stepped beyond that ordered life, 
though distance does not erase the pull of home. A 
Warlock brings a different history: the experience of 
a former warrior joined to the psychic disciplines of 
a seer. Neither role makes every decision certain, 
nor every relationship with another species 
impossible.
To human companions, an Aeldari's priorities may 
seem remote. Make those priorities concrete: a 
threatened spirit stone, a warning only partly 
understood, a debt to someone long dead. Decide 
what would persuade your character to explain 
themselves rather than simply expect obedience. 
Trust gained across that distance should matter.

3 Species
Species have distinct identities, with species-specific 
armour modification rules in Chapter 9 providing 
additional mechanical distinction.
Species defines a character’s physical baseline, cultural 
assumptions, and class access. Each species is
written in the same format for ease of use at the table.
Darkvision. Within the range listed in your species traits, 
you treat dim light as bright light and darkness as dim 
light. In darkness, you see only shades of grey. 
Darkvision does not let you see through smoke, solid 
objects, or psychic darkness unless its rules explicitly 
state otherwise.
If you gain darkvision from more than one source, use 
the longest range; the ranges do not add together. 
Humans, Ogryn and Skitarii have no default species 
darkvision and must obtain it through equipment or 
augmetics, such as the Optical Implant.
3.1 Human
Humans are the baseline of the Imperium: adaptable, 
ambitious, fragile, and dangerously determined.
Ability Scores: +2 to one ability score and +1 to 
another.
Size: Medium.
Speed: 30 ft.
Available Classes: Veteran, Zealot, Psyker, Arbites 
Enforcer, Hive Scum.
3.1.1 Human Traits
Imperial Adaptability: Gain proficiency in one skill of 
your choice.
Broad Training: Gain one additional weapon, tool, or 
language proficiency.
Faith, Fear, or Discipline: Once per long rest, when you 
fail a saving throw, you may reroll it. You must
use the new result.
3.2 Ogryn Abhuman
Ogryns are massive abhumans used by the Imperium as 
shock troops, bodyguards, line-breakers, and
living siege weapons. They are loyal and terrifyingly 
durable, but they are not subtle and struggle with
equipment designed for normal human frames.
Ability Scores: +2 Strength, +1 Constitution.
Size: Medium, but you count as one size larger for 
carrying, lifting, pushing, dragging, grappling, and
shoving.
Speed: 30 ft.
Available Classes: Ogryn Skullbreaker only.
3.2.1 Ogryn Traits
Massive Build: Your maximum hit points increase by 3 
per character level. You also count as one size
larger for carrying, lifting, pushing, dragging, grappling, 
and shoving.
Thick Skull: You have advantage on saving throws 
against being frightened.
Brute Strength: Your unarmed strikes deal 1d6 + your 
Strength modifier bludgeoning damage.
Too Big for Standard Kit: You cannot use most 
standard armour, delicate weapons, compact firearms,
or subtle tools unless they have been modified for Ogryn 
use.
Simple Solutions: You are not automatically stupid, but 
you struggle with delicate logic, subtle
interfaces, encrypted systems, and advanced technology. 
You have disadvantage on Intelligence checks
involving advanced technology, forbidden lore, cogitators, 
security systems, encrypted data, or complex
machinery unless you are proficient in a relevant skill or 
tool. However, once per short rest, when a
problem could plausibly be solved through brute force, 
intimidation, endurance, or direct action, you
may add your proficiency bonus to the check even if you 
would not normally be proficient.
3.3 Ratling Abhuman
Ratlings are small abhumans known for stealth, 
marksmanship, scavenging, cooking, black-market
dealings, and improbable survival.
Ability Scores: +2 Dexterity, +1 Wisdom.
Size: Small.
Speed: 25 ft.
Available Classes: Ratling Sharpshooter, Veteran, Hive 
Scum.
3.3.1 Ratling Traits
Darkvision: You have darkvision to a range of 60 ft (see 
the rules at the start of this chapter).
Small Target: When you have light cover, you may treat 
it as heavy cover.
Sniper’s Eye: You ignore disadvantage from attacking at 
long range with weapons that have the
Accurate property.
Naturally Sneaky: You gain proficiency in Stealth.
Lucky Shot: Once per short rest, when you miss with a 
ranged weapon attack, you may reroll the
attack.
Bad in a Straight Fight: You have disadvantage on 
Strength checks made to shove or grapple creatures
larger than you.
3.4 Skitarii Augmented Human
Skitarii are cybernetically enhanced soldiers of the 
Adeptus Mechanicus. They are machine-disciplined,
sensor-linked, and doctrinally conditioned beyond normal 
human limits.
Ability Scores: +2 Dexterity or Intelligence, +1 
Constitution.
Size: Medium.
Speed: 30 ft.
Available Classes: Skitarii Veteran.
3.4.1 Skitarii Traits
Augmetic Body: You have resistance to poison damage 
and advantage on saving throws against

disease.
Machine Discipline: You have advantage on saving 
throws against being charmed.
Noospheric Focus: Gain proficiency in Investigation, 
Perception, or Technology.
Integrated Auspex: Once per short rest, as a bonus 
action, choose one creature within 60 ft that you
can see. Your next attack against that creature before 
the end of your turn gains +1d4 to hit.
Cybernetic Maintenance: During a short rest, if you or 
an ally has tinker’s tools or Mechanicus tools,
you may regain additional hit points equal to your 
proficiency bonus.
No Psychic Potential: You cannot choose the Psyker 
class or any trait that grants psychic powers.
3.5 Squat / Kin
Squats, often known as Kin in modern Imperial records, 
are hardy void-adapted abhumans associated
with holds, guilds, oath-bands, mining fleets, mercenary 
contracts, and ancient grudges. They are
shorter than humans but dense, resilient, technically 
minded, and extremely difficult to intimidate.
Ability Scores: +2 Constitution, +1 Intelligence or 
Wisdom.
Size: Medium, but your height is usually between 4 and 5 
ft.
Speed: 25 ft.
Available Classes: Kin Armsman, Hernkyn Prospector.
3.5.1 Squat / Kin Traits
Darkvision: You have darkvision to a range of 60 ft (see 
the rules at the start of this chapter).
Dense Build: You have advantage on saving throws 
against being shoved, knocked prone, or moved
against your will.
Void-Hardened: You have advantage on saving throws 
against exhaustion caused by poor atmosphere,
bad rations, forced marches, cramped voidship 
conditions, mining hazards, or environmental hardship.
Guild-Craft: Gain proficiency in Technology, 
Investigation, or one artisan/tool proficiency related to
engineering, mining, weapons, armour, or voidcraft.
Grudge Memory: Once per long rest, when a creature 
damages you or an ally within 30 ft, mark that
creature as the subject of a grudge. The first time you hit 
that creature before the end of the encounter,
add your proficiency bonus to the damage.
Stubborn Kin: You have advantage on saving throws 
against being frightened.
3.6 Aeldari / Eldar
Aeldari are ancient xenos whose reflexes, senses, and 
psychic presence far exceed human norms. Player
Aeldari should represent rare outcasts, rangers, corsair-
adjacent wanderers, or warlocks operating
under a specific hidden purpose.
Ability Scores: +2 Dexterity, +1 Intelligence or Wisdom.
Size: Medium.
Speed: 35 ft.
Available Classes: Aeldari Outcast, Aeldari Warlock.
3.6.1 Aeldari Traits
Darkvision: You have darkvision to a range of 90 ft (see 
the rules at the start of this chapter).
Inhuman Grace: Gain proficiency in Acrobatics or 
Stealth.
Keen Senses: Gain proficiency in Perception. If you 
already have Perception proficiency, add +1 to
Perception checks instead.
Battle Trance: You may move through the space of 
allied creatures without treating it as difficult
terrain. Once per short rest, when you move at least 10 ft 
before making a weapon attack, add +1d4 to
the attack roll.
Ancient Mind: You have advantage on saving throws 
against being charmed or frightened by non-psychic 
effects.
Xenos Distrust: You have disadvantage on Persuasion 
checks with most Imperial authorities unless
disguised, vouched for, or operating under an established 
truce.

SECTION 04
Origins
The transport clerk calls your birthplace a recruitment category. To you it is the smell of hot metal, the 
sound of a prayer before dawn, or the vibration of engines beneath a childhood bunk. A name on a form 
cannot contain those things.
When the mission becomes unfamiliar, old habits return. You count exits, offer the greeting of a distant 
shrine, or search for a horizon that the hive never had. Home can prepare you for danger and leave you 
blind to it. You will discover which lessons travel well.

4 Origins
Origins are narrative-and-proficiency packages. Their 
function is explicitly separate from the universal Trait 
choice made during character creation.
Origins represent upbringing, culture and previous life before becoming part of the warband.

4.1 Hiveborn
Raised in the brutal density of a hive city.
Allowed Species: Human, Ratling, rare Ogryn.
Skill Proficiency: Choose one from Deception, Insight, 
Intimidation, Sleight of Hand, or Stealth.
Crowd Rat: You ignore difficult terrain caused by 
crowds, rubble, cramped spaces, pipes, gantries, and
dense urban clutter.
Seen Worse: You have advantage on saving throws 
against fear caused by gore, violence, intimidation,
or battlefield horror.
4.2 Shrine Worlder
Raised in devotion, ritual, sacrifice, and Imperial worship.
Allowed Species: Human, rare Ratling.
Skill Proficiency: Religion and either Persuasion or 
Intimidation.
Litany of Resolve: Once per long rest, you can give 
yourself or one ally within 30 ft. advantage on a Wisdom 
saving throw.
Sacred Hatred: Once per turn, when you damage a 
heretic, daemon, mutant, witch, traitor, or xenos with
a weapon attack or class feature, you deal an additional 
1d4 + 1 radiant damage.
This damage represents zeal, ritual fury, and trained 
hatred rather than true divine magic.
4.3 Penal Worlder
A convict, survivor, conscript, or former prisoner.
Allowed Species: Human, Ogryn, Ratling.
Skill Proficiency: Survival and one of Athletics, 
Deception, or Intimidation.
Hard Time: You have advantage on saving throws 
against exhaustion caused by forced marches,
starvation, poor conditions, or sleep deprivation.
Dirty Survival: Once per long rest, when you are 
reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, you
may drop to 1 hit point instead.
4.4 Voidborn
Born aboard a voidship, orbital station, warship, pilgrim 
vessel, or ancient wreck.
Allowed Species: Human, Ratling, rare Ogryn.
Skill Proficiency: Choose one from Acrobatics, 
Perception, Investigation, or Technology.
Void Legs: You have advantage on checks and saving 
throws to avoid being knocked prone or moved
against your will.

Combat Rules
The street goes quiet a moment before the firing starts. A window flashes. Stone chips sting your cheek,

6 Combat Rules
“Find cover before you find courage. The enemy will give 
you time for neither.” — Veteran’s field advice
Combat uses the familiar d20 round structure, but Dark 
Imperium assumes firearms, cover, suppression and 
objective play are common rather than exceptional.
6.1 Turns and Actions
On your turn, you may move up to your Speed and take 
one action. A feature may also grant a bonus action. You 
have one reaction between the start of your turn and the 
start of your next turn.
Common 
Action Use
Attack Make weapon attacks allowed by your 
class features and equipment.
Dash Move up to your Speed again.
Disengage Your movement does not provoke 
opportunity attacks this turn.
Dodge
Until your next turn, attacks you can see 
have disadvantage against you, and you 
have advantage on Dexterity saves.
Help
Give an adjacent or plausibly assisted ally 
advantage on one appropriate check or 
attack.
Hide Attempt to become hidden when terrain, 
darkness or concealment allows it.
Ready
Choose a perceivable trigger and an 
action or movement to resolve with your 
reaction.
Reload Reload a weapon when its Reload 
property requires it.
Use Mission 
Gear
Operate a med-pack, auspex, demolition 
tool or other item whose rule requires an 
action.
6.2 Cover
Cover Effect
Light Cover +2 AC against attacks that pass 
through the cover.
Heavy Cover +5 AC against attacks that pass 
through the cover.
Full Cover Cannot be directly targeted through the 
obstruction.
Examples: crates, railings and pipework are usually Light 
Cover; barricades, firing ports and armoured machinery 
are usually Heavy Cover; sealed walls and complete 
corners provide Full Cover. The GM decides whether a 
line of fire crosses the cover.
6.3 Suppression
Some weapons and class features can Suppress a 
target. When a creature is required to make a 
Suppression save, use the attacker's weapon save DC: 8 
+ proficiency bonus + the ability modifier used for the 
attack. A creature that fails is Suppressed until the start 
of the source's next turn unless a rule gives a different 
duration.
● Disadvantage on ranged weapon attacks.
● Cannot willingly move closer to the source of 
Suppression.
● Cannot take reactions.
A creature behind Full Cover from the source 
automatically ends Suppression if the source can no 
longer threaten its position, at the GM's discretion.
6.4 Reload
A weapon with Reload X can normally make X attacks 
before it must be reloaded. Reloading uses an action 
unless a class feature, trait or item says otherwise. 
Reload X represents the current magazine, cylinder, 
charge pack or power cell, not the character's total 
ammunition. In standard play, ordinary spare ammunition 
is abstracted, and a character is assumed to carry 
enough routine reloads for the mission unless the GM 
says scarcity matters. Ammo Packs in Chapter 17 are 
used when ammunition is limited, an emergency resupply 
is needed, or specialist ammunition must be restored. 
Survival-focused campaigns may instead use Supply 
States from the GM Guide.
6.5 Close-Quarters Shooting
Making a ranged weapon attack while a hostile creature 
is within 5 ft normally imposes disadvantage. A weapon 
with the Close-Quarters property ignores this 
disadvantage. Pistols may be drawn and fired in melee 
unless another rule prevents it.
6.6 Critical Hits
On a natural 20 with an attack roll, roll the attack's 
damage dice twice and add modifiers once. Properties 
such as Brutal or Chain may add further dice. Effects that 
trigger on a critical hit resolve after confirming the hit.
6.7 Dropping to 0 Hit Points
At 0 hit points, you fall unconscious unless a feature says 
otherwise. At the start of each of your turns, make a 
death saving throw. On 10 or higher, gain one success; 
on 9 or lower, gain one failure. Three successes stabilise 
you. Three failures kill you. A natural 20 restores 1 hit 
point; a natural 1 causes two failures. Taking damage at 
0 HP causes one failure, or two if the damage came from 
a critical hit.
6.8 Stabilising and Recovery
A creature within reach can use an action and succeed 
on a DC 10 Medicine check to stabilise a dying creature. 
Field dressings, med-packs and class features may 
improve this. Ordinary hit-point recovery follows the 
normal rest rules; lasting injuries, surgery and limb 
replacement use Chapter 19.
6.9 Ranged Attacks and Range
A weapon range written as two numbers, such as 80/240 ft, lists its normal range first and maximum range second. 
Attacks made at or within normal range are resolved normally. Attacks beyond normal range and up to maximum range 
are made with disadvantage. A target beyond maximum range cannot be attacked with that weapon. Area weapons 
that list a cone, line or radius use that listed area instead of normal range bands unless their profile says otherwise.

6.10 Opportunity Attacks
When a hostile creature you can see leaves your melee reach using its own movement, you may use your reaction to 
make one melee weapon attack against it immediately before it leaves your reach. A creature that takes the Disengage 
action does not provoke opportunity attacks for the rest of that turn. Forced movement, teleportation and movement 
that does not use the creature's own Speed do not normally provoke opportunity attacks. Ranged weapons cannot 
normally make opportunity attacks unless a feature specifically allows it.
6.11 Grappling and Shoving
If you can make more than one attack with the Attack action, a grapple or shove may replace one of those attacks. You 
must have at least one free hand to grapple a creature.
Maneuver Procedure
Grapple
Choose a creature within your reach that is no more than one size larger than you. Make a 
Strength (Athletics) check contested by the target's Strength (Athletics) or Dexterity (Acrobatics). 
On a success, the target is grappled.
Escape
A grappled creature may use its action to repeat the contest. On a success, the grapple ends. 
The grapple also ends if the grappler is incapacitated or the creatures are moved beyond the 
grappler's reach.
Move a Grappled Target When you move, you may drag or carry a grappled target, but your Speed is halved unless the 
target is at least two sizes smaller than you.
Shove Choose a creature within your reach that is no more than one size larger than you. Make the 
same contested check as a grapple. On a success, either push the target 5 ft or knock it Prone.
6.12 Two-Weapon Fighting
When you take the Attack action and attack with a one-handed Light melee weapon, you may use a bonus action to 
make one attack with a different one-handed Light melee weapon in your other hand. Do not add your ability modifier to 
the bonus attack's damage unless that modifier is negative or a feature says otherwise. Drawing or stowing both 
weapons follows the normal item-interaction limits unless a feature says otherwise.
Light pistols may be carried in either hand, but dual-wielding pistols does not by itself grant an additional attack. A 
feature that grants a bonus-action pistol attack, such as a Gunslinger or Talent feature, may use either ready pistol. 
Reload each firearm separately. Carrying a pistol and a blade likewise grants no extra attack unless a feature provides 
one.
6.13 Rest and Recovery
Rest Duration Effect
Short Rest At least 1 hour
A period of relative safety with no strenuous activity. You may spend Hit Dice; for each 
die spent, roll it and regain HP equal to the result + your Constitution modifier. Recover 
features that say they return on a short rest. Warp Pressure is reduced to 0 as described 
in Chapter 15.
Long Rest At least 8 hours
At least 6 hours should be sleep or an equivalent species-appropriate rest unless the 
GM rules otherwise. Restore all lost HP, recover long-rest features and regain spent Hit 
Dice up to half your total Hit Dice, minimum one. Warp Pressure is reduced to 0. A 
character can normally benefit from only one long rest in 24 hours.
Rest does not remove Corruption, lasting injuries, lost equipment or narrative consequences unless a specific rule says 
otherwise.
6.14 Conditions and Battlefield States
The following definitions apply when a rule gives a creature one of these conditions or states. If a feature gives a more 
specific duration or effect, the specific feature wins.
Condition / State Effect
Blinded You cannot see and automatically fail checks that require sight. Your attacks have disadvantage; 
attacks against you have advantage.
Bloodied You are Bloodied while at or below half your maximum HP. Bloodied is a state, not a condition, 
and has no effect by itself unless a rule refers to it.
Charmed You cannot attack or deliberately harm the creature that charmed you. That creature has 
advantage on social checks made against you.
Frightened
While you can see the source of your fear, you have disadvantage on ability checks and attack 
rolls and cannot willingly move closer to it. A "fear save" is a save made to avoid or end this 
condition.
Grappled Your Speed becomes 0 and cannot benefit from bonuses to Speed. The condition ends if the 
grappler is incapacitated or you are moved beyond its reach.
Hidden
You are unseen and unheard by a creature that has not located you. Attacks against a creature 
you are hidden from normally have advantage. Making an attack normally reveals your position 
after the attack resolves unless a feature says otherwise.
Incapacitated You cannot take actions, bonus actions or reactions.
Invisible
You cannot be seen without a special sense or effect. Your attacks normally have advantage, 
and attacks against you normally have disadvantage. You can still be detected by sound, tracks 
or other evidence.
Poisoned You have disadvantage on attack rolls and ability checks.

Condition / State Effect
Prone
Your only movement option is to crawl unless you spend half your Speed to stand. Your attacks 
have disadvantage. Attacks against you have advantage from within 5 ft and disadvantage from 
farther away.
Restrained Your Speed becomes 0. Your attacks have disadvantage, attacks against you have advantage, 
and you have disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws.
Stunned You are Incapacitated, cannot move and can speak only falteringly. You automatically fail 
Strength and Dexterity saving throws, and attacks against you have advantage.
Suppressed Disadvantage on ranged weapon attacks; cannot willingly move closer to the source of 
Suppression; cannot take reactions. Full Cover may end Suppression as described in 6.3.
Surprised
If the GM determines you were unaware of danger when combat began, you are Surprised until 
the end of your first turn. While Surprised, you cannot move or take actions or bonus actions, 
and you cannot take reactions until that turn ends.
Unconscious
You are Incapacitated, cannot move or speak, are unaware of your surroundings, drop held 
items and fall Prone. You automatically fail Strength and Dexterity saves. Attacks against you 
have advantage, and a hit from within 5 ft is a critical hit.
Exhaustion
Some hazards, drugs and environmental effects cause levels of Exhaustion. Effects are cumulative. Removing one 
level removes only that level and any higher-level effects that no longer apply.
Level Effect
1 Disadvantage on ability checks.
2 Speed halved.
3 Disadvantage on attack rolls and saving throws.
4 Maximum HP halved.
5 Speed becomes 0.
6 Death.
Unless a rule says otherwise, finishing a long rest while you have access to food, water, and a safe place to recover 
removes one level of Exhaustion.

At the sealed door, each traveller notices something different. The soldier studies the firing angles. The

11.1  /  CLASS LORE
Veteran
Veterans carry a regiment's habits long after its colours have vanished from sight. They check the exits, 
recognise an empty charge pack by its weight, and notice when a companion has stopped answering. The 
Imperial Guard draws soldiers from worlds with very different traditions; survival adds lessons no drill ground can 
supply. In a small warband, that experience becomes a responsibility: someone has to judge when to advance, 
when to hold, and when the mission is no longer worth another life.
Shock Trooper
The first through a breach or across an exposed street, a Shock Trooper relies on practised movement and the fire of the 
people beside them. Courage may be little more than doing the next necessary thing while fear insists otherwise.
Marksman
A Marksman learns to wait inside discomfort. A shifting silhouette, a glimpse of equipment or one careless movement can 
settle a long vigil. Away from the firing position, that patience may become watchfulness, reserve, or a reluctance to waste 
anything.
Sergeant
A Sergeant knows which voice will steady a wavering line. Authority may come from rank, experience, or simply being the 
person who remained. The hardest orders are often the quiet ones, given when there is nobody left to promise a clean victory.

11.2  /  CLASS LORE
Zealot
Faith can give a frightened person a language for courage. Across the Imperium, preachers, pilgrims and 
penitents carry beliefs learned in crowded shrines and inherited through generations. A Zealot takes those 
convictions into danger, drawing strength from ritual, sacrifice or the certainty that a duty remains unfinished. In a 
warband, fervour can inspire others, but it also tests how much room the believer leaves for doubt. Decide whom 
your character's faith obliges them to protect, and what act of mercy they would defend even before a harsher 
authority.
Preacher
Words become an anchor amid panic. A Preacher may know a congregation by name, carry a battered devotional book, or 
speak most persuasively when admitting that they are afraid too.
Flagellant
Penance gives suffering a purpose, at least in the penitent’s own eyes. Consider the promise behind that severity, and 
whether a companion might teach them to value survival as well as sacrifice.
Purifier
The Purifier confronts threats with cleansing flame and fierce resolve. Their certainty is most interesting when the people 
needing rescue are close to the danger they have sworn to destroy.

11.3  /  CLASS LORE
Psyker
A human psyker draws upon a realm in which thought and emotion have terrible power. The Imperium needs 
such gifts while fearing what may follow them into reality. Training, sanctioning and constant scrutiny shape many 
survivors; others live with concealment and the knowledge that discovery could end everything. Within a 
warband, trust is earned through restraint as much as spectacle. The disciplines below describe this conversion's 
character roles. The Blank / Null-Bound option is an exceptional accommodation: a true blank suppresses the 
Warp and is not an ordinary spellcasting psyker.
Biomancer
The workings of living flesh become a focus of attention. Healing and alteration carry intimate responsibilities when another 
person must place their body in your hands.
Telekine
Pressure and motion answer the will. A Telekine may practise with small, precise movements to retain control when fear 
demands something far more violent.
Diviner
Glimpses of possible futures rarely arrive with complete explanations. Decide how your seer copes when a warning helps one 
companion but frightens another.
Pyromancer
Fire is both familiar and unforgiving. Ritual restraint, measured breathing or a remembered disaster can give this dangerous 
discipline a personal history.
Malefic-Touched
Contact with darker powers leaves questions that companions may fear to ask. This path concerns perilous proximity to the 
daemonic, never an assurance of mastery.
Blank / Null-Bound
An absence in the Warp can unsettle those nearby. Consider the loneliness of that effect, and the companions who have 
learned to remain beside you.

Below a hive's official maps, survival depends on relationships that administrators rarely acknowledge. Gangers, 
scavengers, smugglers and displaced workers build lives among polluted waterways and failing machinery.

practical knowledge into a warband: which bargain has a hidden price, which doorway is watched, and who will 
remember a favour. Their cynicism need not erase loyalty. Decide who once shared food with your character 
when there was not enough to share.

Reputation can arrive before the first shot. A Gunslinger may cultivate swagger to prevent a fight, or discover that a 
famous name keeps attracting challengers.

accustomed to formal streets overlook.
Chem-User
Combat chems promise strength or clarity at a price. Consider who controls the supply, what rituals surround their use, 
and which risks your character refuses to pass to others.
Sump Ghost
Moving unseen through neglected places takes patience and local knowledge. A Sump Ghost may leave few traces 
while remembering every person who vanished along the same routes.

habits, signalling clearly while keeping the team concealed.

11.11  /  CLASS LORE
Aeldari Outcast
Leaving the ordered Paths of a craftworld offers freedom without removing danger. Rangers and Corsairs 
encounter unfamiliar societies, distant ruins and temptations that disciplined life once held at a distance. Some

Finding a way through danger means noticing what others miss. A guide’s reputation rests on companions arriving safely,

Aeldari Warlock
Warlocks walk the Path of the Seer after earlier experience on the Path of the Warrior. That martial history helps

Protection extends beyond the immediate body. A Spirit Guardian attends to fear, resolve and the spiritual cost of battle, 
keeping watch over companions and the memory of the dead.

15 Perils of the Warp
Psychic power is not normal spellcasting. It is dangerous, 
unstable, and tempting.
15.1 Warp Pressure
A Psyker has a score called Warp Pressure.
Warp Pressure starts at 0.
Whenever you use a psychic power, increase your Warp 
Pressure by that power’s cost.
After resolving the power, roll a d20. If the result is equal 
to or lower than your current Warp Pressure,
Perils of the Warp triggers.
Example:
● Your Warp Pressure is 5.
● You cast Focused Rupture.
● Focused Rupture adds +2 Warp Pressure.
● Your Warp Pressure is now 7.
● You roll a d20.
● On a 1- 7, Perils trigger.

21 Vehicles
“Count the passengers before departure. Count them again before opening the doors.” — Convoy standing order
Vehicles carry a warband through hive arteries, ash wastes and contested ground. These rules cover ground vehicles, 
walkers and low-altitude skimmers at character-encounter scale. Aircraft, voidcraft and super-heavy war engines 
remain mission assets adjudicated by the GM.
21.1 Profiles and Crew
Read a profile: AC protects the hull; HP measures structural damage; DT is its Damage Threshold (21.5); Speed is 
tactical movement in feet per round. Handling modifies driving checks and vehicle Dexterity saves. Crew lists working 
stations; Passengers lists additional seats. Cargo is capacity after the listed occupants and their normal gear.
Vehicles proficiency adds your proficiency bonus to Dexterity (Vehicles) checks and can qualify you for mounted-
weapon attacks. Add proficiency only once, even if another proficiency applies. Anyone may attempt ordinary driving. 
Unfamiliar alien controls require instruction or a compatible interface before use. Technology repairs vehicles; it does 
not replace Vehicles for driving.
Stations: D = driver, G = gunner, L = loader. One conscious driver at the controls is required to move. Other stations 
may remain empty but cannot act. A G operates one weapon at a time; an L may reload a mount. A one-crew vehicle 
lets its driver operate its listed weapon. A passenger must enter a crew station before using it.
Turns: each character keeps their own initiative, action, bonus action and reaction. The vehicle grants no extra turns. 
On their turn, a driver may spend their entire personal movement allowance to move the vehicle up to its Speed, 
without spending an action. The vehicle receives this movement only once per round, even if drivers swap. Riding does 
not spend a passenger’s movement.
Station changes: boarding a stationary vehicle, disembarking or changing to an accessible station costs 10 ft of 
personal movement. A driver who spent their movement cannot then disembark normally that turn. Small and Medium 
creatures use one seat. An Ogryn uses three passenger spaces and needs suitable access and reinforcement. 
Ordinary crew stations require the Ogryn accommodation upgrade; bikes and undersized chassis cannot take it.
21.2 Driving and Movement
Clear roads and ordinary turns need no roll. Follow a physically possible route: a vehicle cannot pass through walls or 
gaps narrower than its hull. Reversing costs double movement. Walkers turn in place; other vehicles need room to turn. 
Rubble, stairs and steep slopes are difficult terrain unless a trait says otherwise. Tactical Speed is not maximum road 
speed. For map space, use 10 × 10 ft for Large, 15 × 15 ft for Huge, and at least 20 × 20 ft for Gargantuan; the GM can 
use the actual hull outline when terrain demands it.

Dangerous Dense wreckage, unstable bridge, hard evasive turn 13

Roll Dexterity (Vehicles) + Handling. Failure ends movement before the hazard; failure by 5 or more also causes a 
collision (21.4). The GM may state a different consequence before the roll. A natural 1 is not an automatic crash; a 
natural 20 cannot make an impossible stunt possible.
A skimmer operates within 10 ft of a supporting surface. It can cross terrain or calm water allowed by its profile but 
cannot climb above a wall to bypass a scene. When its drive fails, it settles onto the surface below; a fall into a chasm 
remains a fall. Falls deal 1d6 bludgeoning per 10 ft, maximum 20d6, ignoring DT; exposed occupants take their own 
falling damage, while enclosed occupants use the wreck rules if the hull reaches 0 HP.

21.4 Collisions
Ram: the driver spends an action, moves at least 20 ft straight using available vehicle movement, and chooses a target 
in the path. It makes a Dexterity save against 8 + the driver’s Dexterity modifier + Vehicles proficiency, if trained. 
Damage is 4d6 bludgeoning for a Large rammer, 6d6 for Huge or 8d6 for Gargantuan. A creature takes half on a 
successful save and moves to the nearest safe space. A vehicle that succeeds avoids the ram if it has a clear path; 
otherwise it fails. Fixed obstacles automatically fail.
On contact the rammer stops. A struck vehicle or solid obstacle deals half the rolled damage back to it. An accidental 
collision deals the full size-based damage to the moving vehicle and obstacle. Apply DT normally. A vehicle can ram 
once per round and cannot also Drive Hard. Hull damage harms occupants only if it causes a wreck.

Damage and Breakdowns
21.5 Hull Damage and Breakdowns
Damage Threshold: total all damage from one hit or effect after resistance, then compare it with DT. Below DT, the 
hull takes no damage. At least DT, apply the full total. DT is a threshold, not damage reduction. Do not combine 
separate attacks to overcome it.
Against a hull, Armour-Breaking also halves DT for that hit, rounded down. It does not reduce AC or bypass Full Cover. 
This extends the Chapter 7 property. Power Field and Monomolecular do not bypass DT unless explicitly stated. 
Personal weapons can harm hulls when they overcome DT.
Vehicles are objects. Hulls are immune to poison, disease, radiation, fear, Suppression and effects that target only 
creatures or minds. Psychic damage cannot harm a hull unless the power explicitly affects machinery or objects. 
Vehicles do not make death saves, recover through rests or benefit from creature-only healing. Drivers and exposed 
occupants suffer conditions normally; their personal resistances do not protect the hull.
Roll one breakdown when a critical hit damages the hull, or when it first reaches half maximum HP or less in an 
encounter. If it begins at half HP or less, roll on its first damaging hit instead. Maximum one breakdown roll per vehicle 
per round; simultaneous triggers give one roll. Critical hits otherwise double damage dice normally.

2 Steering Disadvantage on driving checks and vehicle Dexterity saves until repaired.

use result 2.
4 Hull breach Lose Sealed. One random enclosed occupant position provides only Heavy Cover until 
repaired.

cannot trigger another breakdown. Field or workshop repair clears running-gear, steering or hull-breach damage (21.8). 
Damage Control clears only jams, stalls and fires.
At 0 HP the vehicle is Wrecked: stop movement and disable its mounts. Each occupant makes a DC 13 Dexterity 
save, taking 2d6 bludgeoning on failure or half on success. Conscious occupants may immediately leave into an 
unoccupied space within 5 ft without an action. Anyone remaining must later leave normally or be rescued. Wrecks do 
not automatically explode. Fire or hazardous cargo may create a separately signalled danger.
Uncontrolled movement: when a vehicle would next move without a conscious driver, it coasts straight up to 30 ft, 
limited by the distance it moved last round, then stops. Resolve obstacles as collisions. A new driver at the controls 
before then can prevent the coast. Swapping drivers never grants a second movement allowance in the round.
21.6 Boarding and Disembarking
Boarding in motion: from within 5 ft, spend an action and make DC 13 Athletics or Acrobatics to reach an exposed 
foothold. DC 16 if either vehicle used Drive Hard this round. Failure leaves you where you started; failure by 5 or more 
also puts you Prone in the nearest safe space and deals 2d6 bludgeoning. Closed or locked hatches must still be 
opened or breached. Moving inside then costs normal movement.
Jumping out of a moving vehicle uses the same action, check and failure damage. No check is needed if it has not 
moved since the start of its driver’s last turn. A passing hull may be targeted by an opportunity melee attack as if it were 
a creature; carried occupants do not provoke just because the vehicle moves. Normal creature-only grapples and 
shoves cannot move a vehicle.

22.2 Combat and Positioning
Rule Reference
Normal/maximum range At or within normal range: no penalty. Beyond normal and up to maximum: disadvantage. 
Beyond maximum: cannot attack.
Close-quarters shooting Ranged attacks while a hostile creature is within 5 ft have disadvantage unless the weapon or 
feature ignores it.
Opportunity attack Reaction; one melee attack when a visible hostile creature leaves your reach using its own 
movement. Disengage prevents it.
Grapple Replace one attack; Strength (Athletics) contested by target's Athletics or Acrobatics. Success: 
target grappled.
Shove Replace one attack; same contest as grapple. Success: push 5 ft or knock Prone.
Light / Heavy / Full Cover +2 AC / +5 AC / cannot be directly targeted through the obstruction.
Suppressed Disadvantage on ranged attacks; cannot willingly move closer to source; no reactions.
Critical hit Natural 20 unless a rule expands the range; roll attack damage dice twice and add modifiers 
once.
Reload X The weapon can normally make X attacks before an action is required to reload.
Two-weapon fighting After attacking with a one-handed Light melee weapon, bonus action attack with a different Light 
melee weapon; no positive ability modifier to bonus damage unless a feature says otherwise.

22.9 Vehicle Quick Reference
Use Chapter 21 for the full procedures, breakdown table, vehicle profiles and mounted weapons.
Rule Reference
Normal driving Spend the driver’s personal movement allowance; move up to vehicle Speed once per round. No 
action.
Drive Hard / Evade Driver action. Drive Hard adds Speed; Evade caps movement at half Speed and protects the 
hull. Both penalise attacks from the vehicle.
Fire a Mount One attack or area use per action; each mount once per round. Extra Attack adds no mounted 
shots.
Mounted attack / DC Attack: d20 + Dexterity + proficiency if trained. Save DC: 8 + Dexterity + proficiency if trained. 
Add Dexterity only to attack-roll damage.
Damage Threshold Whole hit after resistance: below DT = no damage; at least DT = full damage. Armour-Breaking 
halves DT, rounded down.
Breakdown Damaging critical hit or first half-HP trigger of encounter. Maximum one roll per vehicle per 
round.
Wrecked at 0 HP Stop, mounts fail. Occupants: DC 13 Dexterity save; 2d6 bludgeoning, half on success. 
Conscious occupants may exit immediately.
Damage Control Action; DC 13 Technology: clear one jam, stall or fire. No HP recovery.
Field repair 10 minutes, tools, kit, DC 13 Technology. Restore 2d6 + Intelligence HP (minimum 1) OR clear 
one persistent breakdown. One attempt between long rests.
Chase contest Pursuing uses driver action. Opposed Dexterity (Vehicles) + Handling; faster current Speed 
adds +2. Winner changes gap 1 band; margin 5+ changes 2.
Passenger protection Closed hull: Full Cover. Exposed: situational Light Cover. Firing port: Heavy Cover until 
occupant’s next turn.
Crew round checklist
• Choose each crew member’s station before the encounter.
• Driver: move once, then choose an action. Announce Drive Hard or Evasive Driving penalties.
• Gunners: check firing arc, line of sight, range, magazine and the mount’s firing limit.
• Resolve damage against DT, then any eligible breakdown or wreck.
• In a chase, resolve route hazards and the pursuit contest at round’s end.
